clue.text: Girl phones about empty shop in a town down under

indicators.note: the girl and the phones together sit around the next piece, so about signals one piece wrapping another

parts.note: Alice is a girl's name
rings means phones, as in calling someone

indicators.note: an empty word has lost its insides, keeping only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A young woman telephones regarding a vacant shop in some Australian town.
explanation.walkthrough: The container is the girl and the phones read together, with the emptied shop sitting at the join between them; 'phones' alone does not wrap it.
explanation.definitionFit: Alice Springs is a remote outback settlement in Australia's Northern Territory, and Australia is nicknamed the land down under.

clue.text: Girl in ideal arrangement will get help in case

indicators.note: the girl is placed inside the rearranged letters, as the word in directs
an arrangement of the word ideal means its letters are put in a new order

parts.note: gal is an informal word for a girl

explanation.surface: A young woman in a perfect set-up will be assisted if needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangement' gives LEAID from the fodder. 'in case' looks like 'just in case', but the case is a court case.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal aid is state funding for lawyers, so it is assistance for someone involved in a court action.

clue.text: Wimbledon champion caught out by another, reportedly

parts.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught, the way a batsman is out

indicators.note: reportedly means the next word is taken as it sounds when spoken, not as spelt

parts.note: another Wimbledon champion, Arthur Ashe, who won the men's singles in 1975

explanation.surface: A tennis winner is dismissed by a rival, so the gossip goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reportedly' turns the surname ASHE into its sound, ASH. Pat Cash won the Wimbledon men's singles in 1987; 'another' champion means one more, Arthur Ashe.
explanation.definitionFit: Pat Cash is an Australian tennis player who took the Wimbledon singles title in 1987.

clue.text: Understood head of yard supporting son, 18

indicators.note: in a down clue, the pieces that support the son sit beneath it, so the son comes first

parts.note: implicit means understood without being stated

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Grasped, the leader of the yard backs his boy.
explanation.walkthrough: '18' points to the answer to 18 Across, EASE. 'supporting' in a down clue puts IMPLICIT and Y beneath S, so S comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something with ease means doing it with no difficulty, which is the same idea as simplicity.

clue.text: Man, us painter, welcoming Rex with it, a collector's item

indicators.note: welcoming means taking someone in, so the painter's surname holds the next letters

parts.note: Man Ray was an American painter and photographer, so his surname is the piece
R stands for Rex, Latin for king, as on coins and royal signatures
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American artist greets the king with something precious to collectors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a person, but with 'us painter' it names the American artist Man Ray; 'welcoming' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A rarity is something uncommon, exactly the kind of scarce piece that collectors seek.

clue.text: Calming words now and then!

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Soothing phrases, used now and again.
explanation.walkthrough: The everyday phrase 'now and then' (occasionally) supplies its two words with 'and' dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Now then is a phrase said to settle someone down or to calm a tense moment.

clue.text: Extra weapon by barrow?

parts.note: a spear is a weapon for throwing or thrusting
a barrow is something used for carrying loads, so it is a carrier; the question mark admits the stretch

explanation.surface: An additional weapon placed beside a wheelbarrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extra' looks like an adjective meaning additional, but it is the stage sense: a non-speaking actor.
explanation.definitionFit: A spear carrier is a minor actor with no lines, the theatre counterpart of a film extra.

clue.text: Wise man in boat, heading off

indicators.note: heading off means the word loses its first letter, the head

parts.note: a coracle is a small round boat made of wicker and hide

explanation.surface: A sage sits in a little boat, setting off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' sounds like departing, but it removes the first letter, C, from CORACLE. A coracle is a small round Welsh boat.
explanation.definitionFit: An oracle is a person of great wisdom whose advice is treated as authoritative.

clue.text: Swagger in clothes making a comeback

indicators.note: making a comeback means coming back, so the word for clothes is read backwards

parts.note: garb means clothes or dress

explanation.surface: A strutting style in outfits that are back in fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making a comeback' looks like fashion returning, but it reads GARB backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Swagger, as a noun, is showy boastfulness, and a brag is a boast.

clue.text: Belt of identical colour brought in

indicators.note: the colour is brought in to the other word, so it sits inside it

parts.note: same means identical
brown is a colour

explanation.surface: A belt in a matching shade has been introduced.
explanation.walkthrough: A Sam Browne is named after a Victorian British army officer; 'brought in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sam Browne is an army officer's waist strap with a supporting shoulder strap.

clue.text: Come out with a mild expression of surprise

parts.note: workers who come out stop working in protest, which is to strike
taken as written
light means mild, as in a light flavour

explanation.surface: Blurt out a gentle exclamation of astonishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come out with' reads as saying something, but 'Come out' is a walkout; 'with' joins it to the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Strike a light is an old-fashioned British exclamation, much like 'goodness me'.

clue.text: Take on equipment

explanation.surface: Accept the gear.
explanation.definitionFit: To tackle a task is to take it on, and fishing tackle is the gear an angler uses.

clue.text: Christian, perhaps one bringing about end to evil

indicators.note: about means around, so the bringer wraps the letter that follows

parts.note: a fetcher is someone who brings things

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A Christian might be someone who brings evil to a close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' looks like a believer but is Fletcher Christian, leader of the mutiny on the Bounty; 'perhaps' marks his first name as one example. 'about' puts L around inside FETCHER.
explanation.definitionFit: Fletcher is the first name of the Bounty mutineer surnamed Christian, so it is a forename that goes with that surname.

clue.text: Fruit shop supplies Asian cooking ingredient

parts.note: a lemon is a citrus fruit
to shop someone is to inform on them, which in slang is to grass

explanation.surface: A fruit store stocks a spice used in Eastern kitchens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shop' looks like a store, but it is the British slang verb for informing on someone, as is 'grass'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemongrass is a fragrant tropical grass widely used to flavour Thai and other South-East Asian dishes.

clue.text: Trendy signs, conspicuous

parts.note: in means fashionable or trendy
evidence means signs or indications

explanation.surface: Fashionable symbols that are easy to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in evidence is clearly visible and noticeable.

clue.text: A contributor to Christian names

indicators.note: contributor to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: One name that helps make up a list of first names.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a girl's first name, which it is, but the definition is just 'A'.
explanation.definitionFit: In old Indian currency, a was the abbreviation for the coin worth one-sixteenth of a rupee.

clue.text: Something one detests, national song about a leader in Africa

indicators.note: about means around, so the song wraps the single letter given next

parts.note: an anthem is a national song
taken as written

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A hated thing: the national song concerning an African chief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is the container signal and 'leader in' takes the first letter of 'Africa' to close the word.
explanation.definitionFit: An anathema is something deeply loathed, a thing a person abhors.

clue.text: Moderate stand (not 50)

indicators.note: not means the number that follows is to be left out of the word

parts.note: an easel is a stand for a painting
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Take a measured stance, short of fifty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not 50' removes L, the Roman numeral, from EASEL.
explanation.definitionFit: To moderate pain or tension is to relieve or lessen it.

clue.text: Ghost commanding a form of respect

indicators.note: a form of the word respect is its letters set out in a new shape

explanation.surface: A phantom that demands deference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a form of' shuffles RESPECT; 'commanding' only links, though it looks like part of the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectre is an apparition or spirit of the dead.

clue.text: Prospector in square close to Trafalgar

parts.note: forty-nine is a square number, seven times seven

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A gold hunter stands in a square near Trafalgar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'square' looks like a town square such as Trafalgar Square, but it is a square number, 49.
explanation.definitionFit: Forty-niners were the gold seekers who rushed to California in 1849.

clue.text: One regarded as mad in northern state

parts.note: to state is to say, or utter

explanation.surface: A lunatic is found in a state up north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'state' looks like a region, but it is the verb meaning to say.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutter is British slang for a crazy or eccentric person.

clue.text: Garment seen in place of worship on chorister

indicators.note: seen in says the answer can be spotted inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A robe is spotted in a church being worn by a choirboy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'place of worship' looks like the clue for CHURCH or CHAPEL, but the letters run across 'worshiP ON CHOrister'.
explanation.definitionFit: A poncho is a cloak like a blanket with a slit for the head.

clue.text: To try to avoid detection in lodge, I prepared to leave

indicators.note: prepared means made ready, so the letters of lodge and I are reworked

parts.note: to go is to leave

explanation.surface: Someone who wants to stay hidden in a lodge gets ready to depart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prepared' gives LIEDOG from the fodder; 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie doggo is a British idiom for keeping still and quiet so as not to be noticed.

clue.text: Figure of importance, but not paperback's central character

indicators.note: but not means the following letter is to be taken away from the word before

parts.note: stature means importance or standing

indicators.note: the central character of a word is its middle letter

explanation.surface: A notable figure, though not the hero of a paperback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'central character' looks like a novel's hero, but it is the middle letter of 'paperback', R, which 'but not' removes from STATURE.
explanation.definitionFit: A statue is a sculpted human figure.

clue.text: Drunkard carrying heroin and crack

indicators.note: carrying means holding something inside, so the drunkard contains the drug

parts.note: a sot is a drunkard
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A drunk has heroin and crack on him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crack' looks like the drug, but it means an attempt, as in 'have a crack'.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a crack at something is having a go or an attempt at it.

clue.text: Upset at charges, attend uninvited

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters of at charges are scrambled

explanation.surface: Annoyed by fees, someone turns up without an invitation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as annoyed at the prices, but it scrambles AT CHARGES.
explanation.definitionFit: To gatecrash is to go to a party or event without being asked.

clue.text: Flat race, maybe, not quite finished

indicators.note: not quite finished means the word stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: a race is an example of a sporting event

explanation.surface: A level race that has not yet quite ended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite finished' cuts the last letter from EVENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Even means level or flat, as in an even surface.

clue.text: Play Prometheus at broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters of Prometheus at are spread into a new order

explanation.surface: A drama about the Greek Titan is aired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' suggests a radio play, but it scrambles PROMETHEUS AT. The answer is Agatha Christie's long-running London play.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mousetrap is an Agatha Christie murder mystery staged continuously in London's West End since 1952.
